scope: Main purpose frames and function-of-an-underlined-part roles (report sections 8b, 8c, 8d). Overall structure is part a.

templates.name: Main purpose: profile of a person, work or institution
Main purpose: literary reaction, mood or trait
Function: example or supporting detail for a claim
Function: set-up or context for what follows
Function: qualification of an earlier description

items.passage: Many plants respond to insect attacks by increasing their production of defensive compounds, but the cues that alert a plant to an attack are not fully understood. Chemical ecologist Heidi Appel and biologist Rex Cocroft tested whether vibrations might be one such cue. Using actuators attached to the leaves of thale cress (Arabidopsis thaliana), they played back recordings of the vibrations that caterpillars produce while chewing. When caterpillars later fed on these plants, the plants produced more chemical defenses than did plants kept in silence. Vibrations from wind or from a harmless insect’s mating call elicited no comparable response.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes research indicating that plants can respond to the vibrations produced by feeding insects.
It explains how caterpillars use vibrations in leaves to find plants with weak chemical defenses.
It discusses a debate about whether laboratory studies of plants reflect what happens in the wild.
It presents findings showing that caterpillars eat less of plants that have been exposed to recorded vibrations.
items.explanation: The text raises an open question (what cues alert a plant to an insect attack), describes Appel and Cocroft’s test of one possible cue, and reports that plants exposed to recorded chewing vibrations produced more chemical defenses, while wind and a harmless insect’s call had no such effect. Choice A sums up that whole study: research indicating that plants can respond to the vibrations of feeding insects.

B.why_wrong: In the text the plants respond to vibrations made by caterpillars; nothing says caterpillars sense vibrations or use them to find plants.

C.why_wrong: No debate is mentioned, and the text never compares laboratory conditions with conditions in the wild.

D.why_wrong: The study measured the plants’ chemical defenses; the text reports nothing about how much the caterpillars ate.

sources.what: Appel and Cocroft 2014, Oecologia 175: 1257–1266: Arabidopsis thaliana leaves fitted with actuators played recorded Pieris rapae chewing vibrations; when later fed on, primed plants had higher glucosinolate and anthocyanin levels than silent-actuator controls; plants distinguished chewing vibrations from wind and leafhopper song
University of Missouri account: Cocroft a professor of biological sciences; actuators attached to leaves with wax; wind and the call of a non-harmful leafhopper did not raise anthocyanin
Heidi Appel described as a chemical ecologist who studies plant-insect interactions

items.notes: Natural science (plant biology). New subject replacing the Kumar and Epley gratitude-letter study. Study-report build as in 1.15: open question, researchers and method, finding, contrast with control cues. Options in the sentence form of the model. Passage 99 words; model 88.
items.rewrite: New subject (Appel and Cocroft 2014, plants primed by recorded chewing vibrations) replacing the gratitude-letter study; no 'To explore why' setup; distractors are a who-senses swap, an invented debate and an unmeasured outcome instead of an opposite finding; denser register.

items.passage: Early in her career, ceramicist Toshiko Takaezu (1922–2011) produced utilitarian wares such as teapots, plates, and bottles. In the late 1950s, however, she came to regard ceramics as artworks meant to be contemplated rather than used, and she subsequently sealed the openings of her vessels, creating hollow sculptures known as closed forms. Before sealing a form, Takaezu often inserted a fragment of clay wrapped in paper; during firing, the paper burned away, leaving a concealed rattle. Takaezu considered the most important aspect of these works to be their interiors, “the dark space that you can’t see.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To trace how Takaezu’s glazes changed after she moved from Hawaii to the mainland
To characterize a kind of ceramic work Takaezu developed and what she valued in it
To argue that Takaezu’s closed forms should be classified as sculpture rather than pottery
To explain how Takaezu designed her rattles to be heard by visitors to her exhibitions
items.explanation: After one sentence on Takaezu’s early functional pottery, the text describes the closed forms she went on to make (sealed vessels, often with a hidden rattle) and ends with what she considered most important about them, their unseen interiors. Choice B covers both parts: the kind of work she developed and what she valued in it.

A.why_wrong: Glazes, Hawaii and any move to the mainland are never mentioned.

C.why_wrong: The text reports how Takaezu came to regard her work; it does not argue for any classification of the closed forms.

D.why_wrong: The rattle is one detail of how a form was made, and the text says nothing about exhibitions or about rattles being designed for visitors.

sources.what: Takaezu (1922–2011): mid-1950s semi-utilitarian teapots, plates and bottle shapes; in the late 1950s embraced ceramics as artworks meant to be seen rather than used; signature closed form made by sealing her pots; paper-wrapped clay inserted before closing burns free in firing and becomes a rattle
Princeton University Art Museum: closed forms seal the emptiness within; a rattle inserted before closing can be heard from within
Takaezu’s assertion that the most important aspect of her closed forms is “the dark space that you can’t see”

items.notes: Humanities (ceramics). New subject replacing Alma Thomas. Profile build as in 1.4/1.10: person and early work, notable change, method, her own view of its significance; no biography arc to an honor. Passage 96 words; cell median 88.
items.rewrite: New subject (Toshiko Takaezu’s closed forms) replacing the Alma Thomas biography arc; key is about the work and her view of it, not a career arc; strawman 'museums should' distractor replaced by a classification stance trap; denser register.

items.passage: Elephants that leave Kenya’s Tsavo East National Park to raid nearby farms threaten the livelihoods of small-scale farmers. Because elephants avoid bees, Lucy King of the conservation organization Save the Elephants and her collaborators tested an unconventional barrier. From 2012 to 2015, beehives were suspended every 10 meters along the boundaries of farm plots near the park, linked by wire so that an elephant pushing through would set them swinging. Roughly 80 percent of the elephants that approached the fenced farms turned away, and selling the honey gave farmers an additional source of income.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To trace the causes of growing conflict between elephants and farmers in Kenya
To suggest that beehive fences could protect crops from a wide range of wild animals
To present a method of keeping elephants off farms and the results of testing it
To describe how farmers near the park learned to keep bees and sell honey
items.explanation: The text states a problem (elephants raiding farms near Tsavo East), describes the beehive fences King and her collaborators tested, and reports two outcomes: most approaching elephants turned away, and honey brought farmers extra income. Choice C names the method and the results of the trial.

A.why_wrong: The text says that elephants raid farms but gives no causes for the conflict and never says it is growing.

B.why_wrong: Only elephants are discussed; nothing suggests the fences would work against other animals.

D.why_wrong: Honey sales are mentioned only as a side benefit in the last sentence, and the text never describes farmers learning beekeeping.

sources.what: King et al. 2017, Conservation Biology: from 2012 to 2015 beehive fences tested on 10 farms of 0.4 ha next to Tsavo East National Park; hives hung every 10 m around each plot and linked with strong wire; conflict between small-scale farmers and elephants
Conservation Evidence summary of the same study: pushing the wire rocked the hives; of 238 elephants approaching fenced farms, 190 turned away (about 80%)
Save the Elephants: elephants avoid bees; elephants turned away 80 per cent of the time; honey sold from the fences generated income; Lucy King heads the Human-Elephant Co-Existence Program

items.notes: Natural science / applied conservation. New subject replacing the Cheonggyecheon restoration (and the stopped attempt's Living Seawalls, whose reported results conflict between sources). Problem, response, results build as in 1.8, but the effort is a field trial rather than a city law, and the key avoids the model's 'an effort ... and some results of that effort' wording. Passage 94 words; model 91.
items.rewrite: New subject (beehive fences against elephants near Tsavo East, King et al. 2017) replacing the Seoul stream project; key reworded away from the official 'effort and some of its effects' frame; distractors are a cause invention, an overreach and a side-detail partial; denser register.

items.passage: Efforts to protect pollinating insects tend to focus on bees, while hoverflies, which resemble small bees or wasps, have received far less attention. That imbalance is hard to justify. In a 2019 study based on radar data, a team including Karl Wotton and Jason Chapman estimated that up to four billion hoverflies migrate over southern Britain each year, carrying billions of pollen grains between Britain and continental Europe. Many hoverflies are also valuable before they can fly: their larvae feed on aphids, crop pests that locally produced hoverflies consume by the trillions annually.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe the radar technology used to track insects that migrate at high altitudes
To compare how effectively hoverflies and bees pollinate crops
To warn that hoverfly populations in Britain have declined in recent years
To argue that hoverflies deserve more attention for the benefits they provide
items.explanation: The text claims that the neglect of hoverflies relative to bees “is hard to justify” and then supports that claim with two benefits from the 2019 study: hoverflies carry billions of pollen grains, and their larvae eat trillions of aphids. Because the author takes a position and backs it with evidence, the purpose is to argue that hoverflies deserve more attention.

A.why_wrong: Radar is mentioned only as the source of the study’s data; the text never describes how the technology works.

B.why_wrong: The text says bees get more attention, not that they pollinate better or worse; no comparison of effectiveness is made.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text concerns a decline in hoverfly numbers; it reports how many migrate each year.

sources.what: Wotton et al. 2019, Current Biology 29: 2167–2173: migrant hoverflies understudied; radar shows up to 4 billion travel over southern Britain each year; they transport billions of pollen grains between Britain and Europe; larvae are biocontrol agents of aphid crop pests; locally produced populations consume 6 trillion aphids
Rader et al. 2016, PNAS: bees are well documented as crop pollinators, while contributions of pollinators other than bees have been little explored
hoverflies (Syrphidae) commonly resemble bees and wasps

items.notes: Natural science. New subject replacing the fish-intelligence myth-busting passage. Argument build: claim of neglect, evaluative judgment, evidence from one study; no myth-busting frame, no two-animal list, no tacked-on 'Clearly' thesis. Passage 93 words; model 76.
items.rewrite: New subject (migrant hoverflies, Wotton et al. 2019) replacing fish intelligence; evaluative claim stated early and supported by one study's findings instead of a myth-busting frame with two animal examples and a tacked-on thesis; denser register.

items.passage:
The following text is from Dorothy Canfield Fisher’s 1917 novel Understood Betsy. Elizabeth Ann, a nine-year-old girl, is traveling to Vermont.

She shrank together in her seat, more and more frightened as the end of her journey came nearer, and looked out dismally at the winter landscape, thinking it hideous with its brown bare fields, its brown bare trees, and the quick-running little streams hurrying along, swollen with the January thaw which had taken all the snow from the hills. She had heard her elders say about her so many times that she could not stand the cold, that she shivered at the very thought of cold weather, and certainly nothing could look colder than that bleak country into which the train was now slowly making its way.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how the January thaw has caused flooding across the Vermont countryside
To show that Elizabeth Ann is looking forward to exploring the winter landscape
To portray Elizabeth Ann’s growing fear as her journey nears its end
To explain why Elizabeth Ann’s elders refuse to travel during cold weather
items.explanation: Elizabeth Ann grows “more and more frightened as the end of her journey came nearer,” finds the winter landscape “hideous,” and thinks nothing could look colder than the “bleak country” the train is entering. Every detail shows her fear rising as she nears her destination, so choice C states the main purpose.

A.why_wrong: It turns the streams “swollen with the January thaw” into flooding, but the text mentions no flood; the thaw is part of the scenery Elizabeth Ann finds hideous.

B.why_wrong: She looks out “dismally” and thinks the landscape “hideous,” the opposite of looking forward to it.

D.why_wrong: Her elders said that Elizabeth Ann could not stand the cold; the text says nothing about the elders’ own travel or feelings about cold weather.

sources.what: text copied from Project Gutenberg eBook #5347, Understood Betsy, chapter II (second paragraph); chapter I: Elizabeth Ann is “a little girl of nine”; chapter II: the train carries her “toward Vermont”
Understood Betsy by Dorothy Canfield Fisher, published in 1917; heroine a girl of nine sent to live with relatives in Vermont
first edition: New York, Henry Holt and Company, 1917, illustrated by Ada C. Williamson (the illustrator named in the Gutenberg text)

items.notes: Literature (novel, public domain, 1917). Excerpt copied exactly (one full paragraph, two sentences). Context line wording is ours. Dorothy Canfield (Fisher) and Understood Betsy appear in no official item of any skill (cb_api grep). Wikipedia dates the novel 1916, probably from its magazine serial; the book edition is Henry Holt, 1917. Earlier excerpt: L. M. Montgomery’s Anne of Green Gables (official 19688783).

fixes: replaced the Anne of Green Gables excerpt (same novel as official 19688783) with a paragraph from Dorothy Canfield Fisher’s Understood Betsy (1917); options, explanation, distractors and sources rewritten; 128 words (models 79, 102, 125); independent blind solve C

items.passage: Between 1875 and 1878, Cheyenne and Kiowa men imprisoned at Fort Marion in Florida produced hundreds of drawings in paper books, many of them sold to tourists as souvenirs. Art historian Joyce M. Szabo has shown, however, that some of these books resulted from more complicated arrangements between artist and patron. <u>In 1877, for instance, Eva Scott Fényes, who taught English to several of the prisoners, commissioned books from the Kiowa artist Zotom and the Cheyenne artist Howling Wolf.</u> Szabo concludes that Fényes largely determined the subjects of Zotom’s drawings, whereas Howling Wolf preferred to choose his own.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It provides an example of the kind of arrangement mentioned in the previous sentence.
It explains why so many of the drawings made at Fort Marion were sold to tourists.
It introduces a claim about Zotom’s drawings that Szabo goes on to dispute.
It describes how Zotom and Howling Wolf chose the subjects of their drawings.
items.explanation: The previous sentence says that some Fort Marion books came from “more complicated arrangements between artist and patron.” The underlined sentence, which begins “for instance,” gives one such case: Fényes commissioning books from Zotom and Howling Wolf. It is an example of the arrangement just mentioned.

B.why_wrong: The first sentence notes that many books were sold to tourists, but the underlined sentence gives no reason for those sales; it describes a commission.

C.why_wrong: Szabo does not dispute the commission; her conclusion in the last sentence builds on it.

D.why_wrong: Who chose the subjects is explained in the following sentence, and there Fényes, not Zotom, largely chose Zotom’s subjects.

sources.what: Fort Marion, St. Augustine, Florida: 72 Southern Plains prisoners 1875–1878; Pratt supplied paper and colored pencils; more than 1,000 drawings identified; booklets given to visiting officers and sold to tourists
the Fort Marion artists were Cheyenne or Kiowa; Eva Scott Muse Fényes commissioned books from Zotom (Kiowa) and Howling Wolf (Cheyenne) in 1877; Szabo, Imprisoned Art, Complex Patronage (2011)

CAA review of Szabo: Scott commissioned the books from Zotom and Howling Wolf in 1877; she taught English to some of the prisoners; Szabo sees a more complex patronage, with Zotom’s subjects largely set by Scott while Howling Wolf preferred to choose his own subjects

items.notes: History / humanities (Plains drawing). New subject replacing Lakota winter counts. General claim (Szabo: complicated artist–patron arrangements), then the example, then Szabo's conclusion about it, so the last sentence does work and nothing dangles. 'Eva Scott Fényes' is the name the Autry and Szabo use; she married Fényes later. Passage 98 words; cell median 75.5.
items.rewrite: New subject (Szabo on the 1877 Fényes commission of Zotom and Howling Wolf drawing books) replacing winter counts; the example now supports a scholar's claim and is followed by her conclusion instead of a dangling final sentence; denser register.

items.passage: Many online services appear to operate entirely through automated software. Behind them, however, people paid by the task often perform work that algorithms cannot yet handle reliably, from flagging objectionable images to captioning videos and proofreading text. <u>Anthropologist Mary L. Gray and computer scientist Siddharth Suri call this largely invisible labor “ghost work.”</u> Drawing on a five-year study of workers in the United States and India, Gray and Suri report in their 2019 book that people who do ghost work typically receive no health benefits and can be dismissed at any time, for any reason or none.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It presents a hypothesis that Gray and Suri’s research was designed to test.
It lists examples of tasks that algorithms cannot yet handle reliably.
It describes the methods Gray and Suri used to study online workers.
It supplies a name for the labor described in the previous sentence.
items.explanation: The previous sentence describes people who, unseen, do tasks that algorithms cannot yet handle. The underlined sentence gives that labor a name, “ghost work,” which the last sentence then uses when reporting Gray and Suri’s findings.

A.why_wrong: The sentence names a kind of labor; it states no hypothesis, and nothing says the research was set up to test one.

B.why_wrong: The examples (flagging images, proofreading) appear in the previous sentence, not the underlined one.

C.why_wrong: The methods (a five-year study of workers in two countries) are given in the following sentence.

sources.what: Ghost Work (2019) by anthropologist Mary L. Gray and computer scientist Siddharth Suri: services of companies such as Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Uber depend on an unseen human workforce doing piecework such as flagging X-rated content and proofreading
book site: workers have no health benefits and can be fired at any time for any reason, or none; invisible labor force
Kirkus review: the book draws on a five-year study of workers in the United States and India; one worker profiled captions videos for the on-demand platform Amara

items.notes: Social science. New subject replacing rogue planets (and the stopped attempt's ecological-trap claim), which also moves the set away from natural science. The underlined sentence attributes the term to named scholars rather than a bare naming line, and the key names its backward link instead of 'names the objects the rest discusses.' Passage 97 words; model 91.

fixes: added the source for “captioning videos” (Kirkus review: a worker who captions videos for the platform Amara)

items.rewrite: New subject (Gray and Suri's 'ghost work') replacing rogue planets; underlined sentence attributes the term to its authors and the key states its link to the previous sentence rather than a thin naming label; denser register.

items.passage: Many theories of language development treat speech that caregivers address directly to children as a principal driver of language learning. <u>Those theories have been shaped largely by studies of middle-class families in Western countries.</u> To examine children’s language environments elsewhere, Marisa Casillas, Penelope Brown, and Stephen C. Levinson analyzed daylong audio recordings of ten children, aged two months to three years, in a Tseltal Mayan village in southern Mexico. The children were rarely spoken to directly, yet indicators such as the timing of babbling and first words suggested that their language development was proceeding successfully.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence?
options: It describes the methods typically used in studies of Western families.
It notes a limitation of the evidence behind the theories mentioned in the previous sentence.
It summarizes the results of the study conducted in the Tseltal Mayan village.
It indicates that most researchers have rejected the theories mentioned in the previous sentence.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents theories that make speech addressed to children a principal driver of language learning. The underlined sentence points out that those theories rest largely on studies of one kind of family, a weakness in their evidence that the Tseltal study then addresses by looking at a very different community.

A.why_wrong: The sentence says whom the studies examined, not what methods they used.

C.why_wrong: The Tseltal results come in the last sentence, not the underlined one.

D.why_wrong: The sentence identifies a gap in the evidence; nothing says that researchers have rejected the theories.

sources.what: Casillas, Brown and Levinson 2020, Child Development: daylong at-home recordings of 10 Tseltal Mayan children aged 0;2–3;0 in southern Mexico; children infrequently directly spoken to; coarse indicators (babbling, first words, first word combinations) suggest they extract the linguistic information they need

Foushee and Srinivasan 2024, PNAS: theories of language development, informed largely by studies of Western, middle-class infants, highlight caregivers’ child-directed language as a key driver of learning

items.notes: Social science (language development). New subject replacing the sloth-sleep study. The limitation is a plain statement about the evidence base, not a 'However, that research examined only ...' sentence, and the following study tests the theories in another setting rather than overturning one number. Passage 95 words; model 90.
items.rewrite: New subject (Casillas, Brown and Levinson's Tseltal recordings) replacing sloth sleep; limitation sentence no longer clones the official 'However, ... only ...' frame; denser register.

items.passage: Sea otters, the smallest marine mammals, lack the insulating blubber of whales and seals, and their dense fur alone cannot keep them warm in cold water. Instead, they rely on a basal metabolic rate roughly three times that predicted for a mammal of their size. But which tissues generate the additional heat? <u>A 2021 study by Traver Wright, a physiologist at Texas A&M University, and his team pointed to skeletal muscle.</u> Muscle samples from otters of various ages showed exceptionally high leak respiration, a process in which muscles consume energy without performing mechanical work, releasing it as heat.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reports a finding that answers the question raised in the preceding sentence.
It describes how the researchers obtained muscle samples from otters of various ages.
It introduces a hypothesis that the evidence in the following sentence calls into question.
It suggests that blubber matters less to marine mammals than scientists once believed.
items.explanation: The sentence before the underlined one asks which tissues produce the otters’ extra heat. The underlined sentence answers it, reporting that Wright’s team pointed to skeletal muscle, and the last sentence gives the evidence for that answer.

B.why_wrong: The text mentions muscle samples only in the following sentence and never says how they were obtained.

C.why_wrong: The following sentence supports the finding about muscle; it does not call it into question.

D.why_wrong: Blubber appears only in the first sentence, to explain why otters need another heat source; the underlined sentence says nothing about its importance to marine mammals.

sources.what: Wright, Davis, Pearson, Murray and Sheffield-Moore 2021, Science 373: 223–225: sea otter basal metabolic rate about three times predicted; tissue-level source unknown; elevated thermogenic muscle leak could account for it; samples from otters of various ages
Texas A&M: Wright a researcher at Texas A&M; dense fur only goes so far; leak respiration lets muscles generate heat without doing work
sea otters, the smallest marine mammals, lack blubber
Tray (Traver) Wright, physiologist trained at Texas A&M, PhD on oxygen storage in diving marine mammals

items.notes: Natural science. Subject kept (judge p 0.5, no subject tell); architecture changed so it no longer mirrors 1.18 line for line: two context sentences before the question, the question asks which tissue, the answer is a short finding, and there is no 'Thus' conclusion. Wright's 2021 affiliation: Department of Health and Kinesiology, Texas A&M (Crossref). Passage 96 words; model 77.

fixes: “Instead, their basal metabolic rate is ...” did not follow from the fur clause; now “Instead, they rely on a basal metabolic rate ...”

items.rewrite: Same subject, rebuilt so it no longer mirrors official 1.18 (context before the question, no 'argue' answer sentence, no 'Thus' close); key and distractors reworded; denser register.

items.passage: Frogs reproduce in a remarkable variety of ways, yet in nearly all species, eggs are fertilized outside the female’s body. As of 2014, <u>fewer than a dozen of the 6,455 recognized frog species were known to fertilize eggs internally, and each of those either laid fertilized eggs or gave birth to froglets</u>. That year, however, zoologist Djoko Iskandar of Indonesia’s Bandung Institute of Technology and two coauthors described the fanged frog Limnonectes larvaepartus, found only on the island of Sulawesi, whose females give birth to live tadpoles and deposit them in slow-moving streams or small pools.
items.stem: Which choice best states the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes how researchers determined the number of frog species that fertilize eggs internally.
It presents a hypothesis about frog reproduction that the discovery of Limnonectes larvaepartus confirmed.
It summarizes the reproductive patterns that Limnonectes larvaepartus was found to depart from.
It accounts for the rarity of internal fertilization among frogs.
items.explanation: The underlined portion sets out what was known as of 2014: the few frogs with internal fertilization all laid eggs or bore froglets. The next sentence, beginning “That year, however,” presents Limnonectes larvaepartus, which breaks from those patterns by giving birth to tadpoles, so the underlined portion summarizes the patterns the new species departs from.

A.why_wrong: The portion states how many species were known to fertilize internally but says nothing about how anyone arrived at that number.

B.why_wrong: The portion gives known facts, not a hypothesis, and the new species contradicts the pattern rather than confirming it.

D.why_wrong: It reports that internal fertilization is rare but offers no reason why.

sources.what: Iskandar, Evans and McGuire 2014, PLOS ONE: Limnonectes larvaepartus, endemic to Sulawesi, unique among frogs in having internal fertilization and birth of tadpoles; fewer than a dozen of 6,455 frog species known to fertilize internally, and all others deposit fertilized eggs or give birth to froglets
Kusrini et al. 2015, PLOS ONE: tadpoles are birthed into slow-flowing streams or small pools next to streams
Djoko Iskandar, zoologist at Institut Teknologi Bandung, Indonesia

items.notes: Natural science. New subject replacing the White Sands footprints. Same move as model 1.2 (known pattern in the underlined portion, then the discovery that breaks it) without its 'Before the discovery, ... were thought' frame or its single long sentence, and the key names the relation ('patterns ... was found to depart from') instead of 'clarifies why the rest of the sentence is notable.' Passage 96 words; model 88.
items.rewrite: New subject (Limnonectes larvaepartus, the tadpole-bearing frog) replacing White Sands footprints; underlined portion states known facts rather than cloning 'Before the discovery, ... were thought'; key no longer 'helps clarify why the rest of the sentence is notable'; denser register.

items.passage:
The following text is from Gene Stratton-Porter’s 1909 novel A Girl of the Limberlost. Elnora Comstock, who lives on an impoverished farm, has just entered the auditorium of the city high school on her first day of classes.

She had two fleeting impressions. <u>That it was all a mistake; this was no school, but a grand display of enormous ribbon bows; and the second, that she was sinking, and had forgotten how to walk.</u> Then a burst from the orchestra nerved her while a bevy of daintily clad, sweet-smelling things that might have been birds, or flowers, or possibly gaily dressed, happy young girls, pushed her forward. She found herself plodding across the back of the auditorium, praying for guidance, to an empty seat.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It implies that the auditorium has been decorated with ribbons for a special occasion.
It conveys how overwhelmed Elnora feels as she takes in the unfamiliar scene.
It indicates that the other students find Elnora’s appearance amusing.
It shows that Elnora is eager to make friends with the girls around her.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence gives Elnora’s two first impressions: the place seems to be no school at all, and she feels that she is sinking and has forgotten how to walk. Both images show how overwhelmed she is by the crowded, unfamiliar auditorium.

A.why_wrong: The “grand display of enormous ribbon bows” is Elnora’s impression of the crowd (the girls’ hair ribbons), not a description of decorations, and no special occasion is mentioned.

C.why_wrong: The sentence reports Elnora’s own impressions; nothing in the excerpt shows how the other students react to her.

D.why_wrong: Elnora feels lost and unsteady; nothing suggests she is eager to make friends, and she goes alone to an empty seat.

sources.what: full text of A Girl of the Limberlost, chapter 1 (four consecutive sentences copied exactly)
A Girl of the Limberlost, 1909 novel by Gene Stratton-Porter; Elnora Comstock, a poor girl from a farm by the Limberlost swamp, attends high school in the town of Onabasha

items.notes: Literature. New excerpt replacing The Call of the Wild (judged a famous excerpt). Neither Stratton-Porter nor this novel appears in any official item or other generated file. Excerpt: four consecutive sentences, exact (checked against Gutenberg #125); context line is ours. The underlined sentence is the original's fragment construction ('That it was all a mistake; ...'). Passage body 86 words, 124 with the attribution; cell median 96 (full passage).
items.rewrite: New, less-anthologised excerpt (Stratton-Porter, A Girl of the Limberlost) replacing The Call of the Wild; distractors are plausible misreadings (literal ribbons, other students' reaction, eagerness) instead of an obvious literal/opposite pair.

items.passage: By the 1960s, the last native speakers of myaamia, the language of the Miami people, had died, a loss accelerated by the nation’s forced removal from its Great Lakes homeland. Beginning in the early 1990s, Daryl Baldwin, a citizen of the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma, nevertheless taught himself and his family the language, relying on linguist David Costa’s analyses of archival documents that included dictionaries compiled by French missionaries. Baldwin subsequently earned a master’s degree in linguistics and in 2001 became founding director of the Myaamia Project at Miami University in Ohio, now a center that develops educational materials with the tribe.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall purpose of the text?
options: To explain why the Miami people were forced to leave their homeland in the Great Lakes region
To compare the methods Baldwin and Costa used to study historical records of myaamia
To show that myaamia has again become the primary language of the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma
To describe Baldwin’s role in reviving a language that had lost its last native speakers
items.explanation: The text first establishes that myaamia had no native speakers left, then follows Baldwin as he learns the language from archival sources and teaches it to his family, then founds the Myaamia Project. Every part concerns his work to bring the language back, so D states the overall purpose.

A.why_wrong: The forced removal is mentioned once, as a cause of the language’s decline; the text gives no reasons for the removal itself.

B.why_wrong: Baldwin relied on Costa’s analyses; the text never sets their methods side by side.

C.why_wrong: The text describes teaching and curriculum work but never claims that myaamia is now the tribe’s primary language.

items.passage: Because details tend to shift each time a story is retold, oral traditions are often dismissed as unreliable records of the distant past. A 2016 study by geographer Patrick Nunn and linguist Nicholas Reid suggests that such skepticism can go too far. Nunn and Reid examined Aboriginal Australian stories from 21 coastal sites, each describing land that is now under the sea, and compared the water depth each account implies with the established record of sea-level rise after the last ice age. By that measure, the stories preserve observations made more than 7,000 years ago. Oral traditions deserve serious consideration as historical evidence.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To argue that oral traditions can be valuable sources of information about the distant past
To explain how rising seas altered the way of life of Aboriginal Australians
To question the accuracy of the sea-level record that Nunn and Reid relied on
To show that oral traditions are generally more dependable than written records
items.explanation: The text names a common view (oral traditions are unreliable), presents Nunn and Reid’s finding that some Aboriginal stories preserve observations over 7,000 years old, and closes with the author’s judgment that oral traditions “deserve serious consideration as historical evidence.” Its purpose is to argue for their value as sources about the distant past.

B.why_wrong: The stories are used as evidence of sea-level rise; the text never discusses how Aboriginal ways of life changed.

C.why_wrong: The sea-level record is the trusted benchmark against which the stories are checked; the text never doubts it.

D.why_wrong: Written records are never mentioned, and the text claims only that oral traditions deserve consideration, not that they are generally more dependable.

items.passage: <u>Many trees reproduce by mast seeding, or masting: individuals across a population synchronously produce enormous seed crops in some years and very few in others.</u> Bumper years satiate seed predators, allowing many seeds to escape consumption. Analyzing nearly four decades of seed production by European beech trees in England, ecologist Michał Bogdziewicz and colleagues found that as the climate warmed, the trees produced more seed overall but varied less from year to year and less in unison, while losses to seed-eating moth larvae climbed. The main beneficiaries of the trees’ increased seed production, the researchers conclude, are not the trees but their predators.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the first sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents a hypothesis about seed predators that Bogdziewicz and colleagues set out to test.
It defines a reproductive pattern whose disruption the text goes on to describe.
It describes a recent change in beech trees’ behavior that the researchers attribute to rising temperatures.
It explains why moth larvae have destroyed a growing share of beech seeds in England.
items.explanation: The first sentence explains what masting is. The text then notes why masting helps trees and reports that, as the climate warmed, beech seed production became less variable and less synchronized, the very features that define masting, while predators gained. So the first sentence defines the pattern whose breakdown the study describes.

A.why_wrong: The sentence describes how many trees reproduce; it is not a hypothesis, and nothing in the text is framed as a test of it.

C.why_wrong: The change linked to warming (less variable, less synchronized seed production) is reported in the third sentence; the first sentence describes masting itself.

D.why_wrong: Rising losses to moth larvae are mentioned only in the third sentence, and the first sentence gives no reason for them.

items.passage: Metamaterials, structures whose unusual physical properties arise from the arrangement of many tiny elements rather than from the materials they are made of, are rare in nature, and until recently no acoustic example was known. Biologist Thomas Neil and colleagues have found that the scale layer on moths’ wings is one: <u>each scale acts as a resonator tuned to a specific frequency, and because the scales are coupled through the wing membrane, together they absorb ultrasound across the full range of frequencies that bats use in echolocation</u>. This acoustic camouflage is achieved with a layer thin and light enough for flight.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the procedure the researchers followed to measure how much ultrasound moth wings absorb.
It qualifies the previous sentence’s claim that acoustic metamaterials are rare in nature.
It explains why bats have been unable to adjust their calls to detect moths in flight.
It explains how moths’ wing scales function together as an acoustic metamaterial.
items.explanation: The first part of the sentence says that the scale layer on moths’ wings is an acoustic metamaterial. The underlined portion explains how it works: each scale resonates at its own frequency, and the coupled scales together absorb the full range of bat frequencies. Choice D names that mechanism.

A.why_wrong: The portion explains how the scales absorb sound, not how the researchers measured that absorption; no procedure is described.

B.why_wrong: The portion does not limit the claim that such structures are rare; it explains how one natural example works.

C.why_wrong: The text never says whether bats can adjust their calls; it describes how the wings absorb ultrasound.

items.passage: Because avian mothers cannot modify their embryos’ biochemical environment after laying, it has been unclear whether birds can prepare their offspring for prevailing climatic conditions. items.passage: The Silk Road is popularly imagined as a highway along which merchant caravans conveyed silk and other luxuries in great volume between China and Rome. But the contracts and other everyday documents preserved in the dry sands of the Taklamakan Desert led historian Valerie Hansen to a far more modest picture: direct commerce between China and Rome was minimal, and most exchange consisted of small-scale transactions among local peddlers. What principally sustained the region’s economy, Hansen contends, was government expenditure, notably the bolts of silk with which the Tang dynasty paid the garrisons stationed on its northwestern frontier.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To present a historian’s reassessment, drawn from everyday records, of the scale and nature of Silk Road commerce
To argue that the Tang dynasty’s spending on its frontier garrisons ultimately disrupted the trade between China and Rome
To describe how documents found in the Taklamakan Desert reveal the routes that caravans followed between China and Rome
To explain how local peddlers distributed the silk that the Tang dynasty used to pay the soldiers on its frontier
items.explanation: The text sets out the popular image of the Silk Road and then presents Hansen’s contrary account, drawn from everyday documents: little direct trade between China and Rome, mostly small local exchanges, and an economy sustained by government spending. Choice A covers both the revision and its documentary basis.

B.why_wrong: The text says direct commerce between China and Rome was minimal; it never claims that garrison spending disrupted such trade.

C.why_wrong: Hansen uses the documents to challenge the image of caravans traveling between China and Rome, not to trace their routes.

D.why_wrong: Peddlers and the silk paid to garrisons are two separate details; the text never connects them, and neither is its main concern.

items.passage:
The following text is from Margaret Oliphant’s 1866 novel Miss Marjoribanks. Lucilla Marjoribanks has been refused permission to leave school and manage her widowed father’s household.

Miss Marjoribanks did not by any means learn by this defeat to take the characters of the other personæ in her little drama into consideration, when she rehearsed her pet scenes hereafter—for that is a knowledge slowly acquired—but she was wise enough to know when resistance was futile; and like most people of lively imagination, she had a power of submitting to circumstances when it became impossible to change them. Thus she consented to postpone her reign, if not with a good grace, yet still without foolish resistance, and retired with the full honours of war.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To suggest that Lucilla’s disappointment has finally taught her to consider the wishes of the people around her
To reveal Lucilla’s ambition to perform in theatrical productions once she has completed her schooling
To portray Lucilla as so wounded by her father’s refusal that she abandons her plans for his household
To show that Lucilla, though slow to understand others, knows how to accept a defeat she cannot reverse
items.explanation: The narrator says Lucilla did not learn from this defeat to take other people’s characters into account (“a knowledge slowly acquired”), but that she was “wise enough to know when resistance was futile” and gave way “without foolish resistance.” Choice D captures both the limitation and the good sense.

A.why_wrong: The first clause says she did not learn from the defeat to consider other people’s characters.

B.why_wrong: “Drama,” “rehearsed,” and “scenes” describe how Lucilla imagines her own life; nothing concerns a stage career.

C.why_wrong: She “consented to postpone her reign,” which means delaying her plans, not giving them up, and she yields “without foolish resistance” rather than in hurt.

sources.what: text copied from Project Gutenberg eBook #41286, Miss Marjoribanks, chapter 1 (Lucilla, fifteen, asks to stay home after her mother’s death; her father sends her back to school)
serialized in Blackwood’s Magazine February 1865 to May 1866; book 1866

items.notes: Literature. Two consecutive sentences from the end of chapter 1, copied exactly except that the double hyphens are set as closed em dashes; “personæ” and “honours” as printed. Oliphant is not used elsewhere in the bank or the official items.

fixes: context line trimmed (“fifteen,” dropped) so the full passage is 122 words, the hard-tier official maximum; trimming the excerpt at its only sentence boundary would have cut it to 64 body words and removed the basis for the key and for C

items.rewrite: New, less-anthologised excerpt (Oliphant, Miss Marjoribanks) replacing Teasdale’s much-anthologised poem; distractors are near misses (REV twice, one LIT) rather than each mining one image.

items.passage: For much of the twentieth century, scholars of Hawai‘i relied on a small canon of nineteenth-century Hawaiian writings that had been translated into English. M. Puakea Nogelmeier, a scholar of the Hawaiian language, traces this reliance to a “discourse of sufficiency”: the long-standing acceptance of a fraction of the sources as adequate to represent the whole. <u>Hawaiian-language newspapers alone, published from 1834 until 1948, filled some 125,000 pages with news, history, literature, and lore, much of which later scholars left untapped.</u> Moreover, Nogelmeier argues, the translations themselves recast their authors’ self-representations to fit a Western framework.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It presents evidence for the claim, made in the following sentence, that the translations distort how Hawaiian authors represented themselves.
It offers an example that conveys how much material the reliance described in the previous sentence has left out of consideration.
It explains why scholars came to treat a handful of translated works as an adequate basis for their research on Hawai‘i.
It identifies the period during which the canonical translations described in the first sentence were first published in English.
items.explanation: The previous sentence says scholarship accepted a fraction of the sources as enough to represent the whole. The underlined sentence gives one body of sources, the Hawaiian-language newspapers, and its size (some 125,000 pages), much of it untapped, which shows how much that reliance has left out.

A.why_wrong: The size of the newspaper archive says nothing about whether the translations distort their authors; the following sentence adds a separate criticism (“Moreover”).

C.why_wrong: The text never explains why scholars relied on the translations; the sentence describes what they left aside.

D.why_wrong: The dates 1834 to 1948 are when the Hawaiian-language newspapers were published, not when the English translations appeared.

sources.what: Nogelmeier 2003 dissertation (published 2010 as Mai Pa‘a i ka Leo, Bishop Museum Press): “discourse of sufficiency” means modern scholarship has long accepted a fraction of the available sources as sufficient to represent the whole; 20th-century English translations became a reference canon; newspapers published from 1834 until 1948 produced about 125,000 pages, a repository for news, history, literature and lore, left untapped; the translated canon recasts auto-representational writings into a modern Western framework
dissertation record and abstract (University of Hawai‘i at Mānoa, 2003)

items.notes: Humanities (historiography). The underlined sentence is an example of the neglected sources, set between the concept and a further criticism, unlike the term-then-literary-synopsis frame of model 3.5.
items.rewrite: New subject (Nogelmeier’s discourse of sufficiency and the Hawaiian-language newspapers) replacing Shklovsky and Kholstomer; no theory-term-then-literary-example frame; distractors include a wrong-pointer near miss and a misread date.

items.passage: Rock varnish is a dark coating that forms on exposed rock surfaces in deserts worldwide. <u>Its most perplexing feature is its composition: varnish typically contains two to three orders of magnitude more manganese than the underlying rock or the surrounding dust from which much of its mass derives.</u> Analyzing varnish from the western United States, geobiologist Usha Lingappa and colleagues found it rich in cyanobacteria of the genus Chroococcidiopsis. These microbes stockpile manganese inside their cells, apparently using the metal as an antioxidant. Such uptake by the coating’s pioneer microbes, the researchers propose, accounts for its enrichment.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies a puzzling property of a material that the research described in the rest of the text helps account for.
It presents a hypothesis about the source of varnish’s manganese that Lingappa and colleagues’ analysis ultimately refuted.
It explains why rock varnish forms only on the exposed rock surfaces of the deserts mentioned in the previous sentence.
It describes the method by which Lingappa and colleagues measured the manganese content of the varnish samples they collected.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence calls varnish’s manganese content its “most perplexing feature.” The rest of the text reports Lingappa and colleagues’ finding that manganese-hoarding cyanobacteria live in varnish and their proposal that this uptake explains the enrichment. So the sentence sets up the puzzle the study helps explain.

B.why_wrong: The sentence states an observed property, not a hypothesis, and the study explains the enrichment rather than refuting anything.

C.why_wrong: The sentence is about varnish’s composition; it gives no reason for where varnish forms.

D.why_wrong: The sentence reports a typical manganese level, not how the researchers measured it; no method is described.

sources.what: Lingappa et al. 2021, PNAS 118(25) e2025188118: desert varnish is a dark rock coating that forms in arid environments worldwide; most perplexing aspect is its manganese enrichment, two to three orders of magnitude above underlying rocks or the surrounding dust from which much of its mass originates; samples from sites across the western United States; abundant Chroococcidiopsis cyanobacteria accumulate extraordinary intracellular manganese, apparently as a catalytic antioxidant; enrichment related to uptake by likely founding members of varnish communities
Caltech record of the paper

items.notes: Natural science (geobiology). Usha Lingappa, Caltech; senior author Woodward Fischer.
items.rewrite: New subject (rock varnish manganese and Chroococcidiopsis, Lingappa et al. 2021) replacing the Kangaroo Island wallabies; underlined sentence sets up a puzzle instead of cloning the official ‘can persist long after’ generalization; stem changed from the model’s ‘third sentence’ wording.
